sections.body: Client intake and triage covers the initial capture, conflict checking, matter classification, urgency assessment, and routing of new legal work requests. It sits between business development, compliance, and practice teams, and determines which matters are accepted, declined, or referred. In legal operations, this includes standardizing intake forms, matter types, and service-level expectations before a lawyer is assigned.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on matter management platforms, CRM systems, document intake portals, and workflow automation tools connected to conflicts databases and billing systems. Many teams use cloud-based intake queues with role-based access, e-signature capture, and API links to practice management software. The site tracks 732 AI tools, some of which now assist with intake classification, but core infrastructure remains the system of record for matters and parties.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: Intake staff and automated workflows collect party names, matter description, jurisdiction, deadlines, and fee arrangements, then run conflict searches against existing client and adverse party lists. Triage rules sort requests by practice area, urgency, and capacity, often using checklists or decision trees. AI is increasingly used to extract entities from emails and documents, suggest matter codes, and flag missing information before human review.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Client intake carries confidentiality, conflicts of interest, data protection, and records retention obligations. Provenance matters because intake data feeds conflict clearance, engagement letters, and billing, so the source and timestamp of each field should be preserved. Risk controls include access restrictions, audit logs, and human sign-off for high-risk or unclear matters, while automated decisions should be explainable and reversible.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Intake and triage are moving toward more unified intake layers that connect email, web forms, and portals to matter management with less manual rekeying. Teams are testing AI for preliminary conflict flagging, urgency scoring, and routing suggestions, with a human reviewer kept in the loop. The likely direction is faster, more consistent intake that still preserves the conflict and confidentiality checks legal work requires.
